To complement the time-resolved Bayes factors with a test that does not depend on sample-bysample inference, we performed a cross-validated peak test (Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023) on the regression coefficients. Participants were split into four folds. For each fold, the timepoint with the largest absolute group t-value within the post-stimulus window (0-1500 ms) was identified from the remaining three folds, and the held-out participants' coefficients at that timepoint were retained. The retained values were pooled across folds and summarised with a t-statistic. Significance was assessed against a null distribution generated by repeating the procedure on 5000 sign-flipped datasets, in which each participant's whole coefficient time course was randomly multiplied by ±1.

Results

The pupil singles out illusory faces

Pupil responses to the three categories were not simply graded; human faces and non-face objects both produced a constriction relative to pre-stimulus baseline, whereas illusory faces had the opposite effect: a stimulus-evoked dilation (Figure 2A). There were also marked effects of image luminance (Figure 2B), whereas pupil diameter did not vary obviously with emotional valence (Figure 2C). Notably, these marked pupillary responses to stimulus characteristics peaked approximately 600 ms after image onset, despite new images being presented every 267 ms. Thus, despite the relatively slow dynamics of the pupil response, information about individual stimuli could be recovered from temporally overlapping pupillary responses. This observation highlights the potential utility of pupillometry for investigating perceptual processes under rapid visual presentation conditions. Note. Change in pupil diameter as a function of category, luminance and valence; see statistical results in Figure 3. A) Mean pupil diameter change in response to different image categories. Illusory faces resulted in dilation, whereas human faces and non-face objects resulted in constriction. B) Luminance effects were very clear in the pupil response, with graded effects of pupil dilation/constriction based on mean stimulus luminance. C) Emotional valence of the images, as rated by a different group of participants, influenced the pupil response to a lesser extent than the other factors.

To assess how pupil responses varied with image category, we performed a rank regression with category pairs as predictors, as well as rank-transformed luminance and valence ratings to control for features that have been previously shown to influence pupil size (Mathôt, 2018). Indeed, rather than falling between human faces and objects, the pattern expected if the pupil tracked position along a face-likeness continuum, illusory faces produced a reliably larger response than both human faces and non-face objects (Figure 3). Both illusory contrasts were highly reliable (illusory face vs non-face object: peak β = 0.009 at 705 ms, BF = 6.2 × 10 8 ; illusory face vs human face: peak β = 0.008 at 593 ms, BF = 1.5 × 10 4 ). By contrast, there was a much smaller and later difference between faces and objects, (max β = 0.004, BF = 4.07, 893 ms), and this effect did not reach significance using the cross-validated peak test (t = 2.20, p = .070). The pupil thus largely singles out the ambiguous illusory category from both unambiguous ones. These category effects were reliable despite controlling for a large influence of luminance on pupil response (max |β| = -0.033, BF = 6.6 × 10 17 , 541 ms) and a smaller effect of valence (max β = 0.001, BF = 3.37, 453 ms). The cross-validated peak test confirmed significant effects of both illusory contrasts (illusory face vs non-face object: t = 8.99, p < .001, mean peak latency = 694 ms; illusory face vs human face: t = 5.45, p < .001, 541 ms), as well as the effects of luminance (t = -17.92, p < .001, 520 ms) and valence (t = 2.86, p = .015, 457 ms). Note. Beta values from rank regression with five predictors. Bayes Factor plots underneath indicate Wmepoints with reliable evidence (BF > 3); see text for cross-validated peak tests. Markers are coloured by the strength of the evidence: BF<1/3 in grey as evidence for no effect, BF>3 coloured as evidence for an effect, and open circles as insufficient evidence.

The pupil response scales with the strength of the face percept in illusory faces

Having shown a reliable illusory dilation in the pupil that is independent from luminance and valence, we next asked what the dilation reflects. The pupil's non-luminance response is a broad index of arousal, and there are several candidate mechanisms: perceptual conflict between the object and face interpretations, attentional capture, and processing effort. These are not fully separable by pupillometry alone, because each can act through overlapping arousal systems. What our design does allow is a set of graded tests, using behavioural measures of the same images, that constrain which of these mechanisms is plausible.

The response scales with the face percept.

To ask how the dilation scaled within the illusory category, we regressed the pupil response to each of the 100 illusory images on two properties of that image, leveraging data from Robinson et al. (2025): rated face-likeness (how strongly the image is seen as a face) and the proportion of "face" responses under speeded face/object categorisation (how far the face wins the decision). Again, we controlled for emotional valence and luminance. Illusory faces were rated as highly face-like (mean rating = 6.93 on a 0-10 scale) yet overwhelmingly categorised as objects (mean proportion "face" = 0.10), but with reliable image-to-image variation.

Both face-percept measures were positively related to the pupil response (Figure 4). Face-object categorisation was the stronger and more reliable predictor: its coefficient was positive and reliable between 585-825 ms (peak β = 0.003 at 709 ms, BF = 37.2), and this was confirmed using the crossvalidated peak test (t = 3.49, p = .002, mean peak latency = 691 ms). Face-likeness was associated with a broader and more variable pupil response, peak β = 0.003, BF = 5.38 at 641 ms, and this effect did not reach significance using the cross-validated peak test (t = 2.31, p = .060, 776 ms). Illusory images that were more oPen categorised as faces thus produced larger pupil dilaNons, with weaker evidence for a similar relaNonship with rated face-likeness. Note that these face percept behaviours were collected in independent subjects from the pupil data, and thus a relationship between the behavioural judgements and pupil response indicates a reliable stimulus-based effect that is robust across people.

Together the positive pupil-behaviour relationships are consistent with a perceptual-conflict account. Every illusory image here was reliably categorised as an object; the images vary in how strongly the competing face interpretation intruded. The images that come closest to being categorised as faces, are those in which the face interpretation most strongly contests an object decision, and pupil dilation scaled with this conflict. Note. Results from rank regression performed on pupil response to the 100 illusory face images. Beta values are shown for the two behavioural tasks (face-like scores, face-object categorisation) after controlling for image luminance and emotional valence. Bayes Factor plots underneath indicate Wmepoints with reliable evidence (BF > 3); see text for crossvalidated peak tests. Markers are coloured by the strength of the evidence: BF<1/3 in grey as evidence for no effect, BF>3 coloured as evidence for an effect, and open circles as insufficient evidence.

The response does not track valence.

In the same model, ratings of emotional valence showed no reliable relationship with the pupil response at any timepoint (peak |β| = -0.001 at 817 ms, BF = 0.02), despite ample image-to-image variation (emotional valence of the illusory face images ranged approximately 3.2-7.1, M = 4.9, a similar range to the face and object categories) and near-zero correlation with the other predictors. Because valence carried real variance yet did not move the pupil where the face-percept measures did, this argues specifically against an interest or appraisal account, on which the response would reflect how the image is evaluated once recognised rather than the processing of the face itself. Luminance, by contrast, was again the dominant influence within the illusory set (peak β = -0.02, BF = 8.26 x 10 14 at 517 ms), consistent with its role across all 300 images.

The effect does not habituate. Across the epoch, the illusory face minus non-face object difference showed no reliable dependence on repetition number (peak |β| = -0.003 at 1141 ms, BF = 0.36) and the cross-validated peak test likewise found no effect (t = -1.23, p = .274). The dilation therefore shows no evidence of being driven by novelty or surprise, both of which we would expect to attenuate with repeated exposure.

Taken together, the illusory-face based dilation scaled with the strength of the intruding face percept, was sustained rather than transient, could not be reduced to novelty or the affective evaluation of the image, and was largest precisely for the one category in which faces are seen but objects are reported. We read this as consistent with the pupil indexing the perceptual conflict between the object and face interpretations.

Discussion

In this study, we set out to ask what the pupil tracks when observers view illusory faces. Across mean pupil responses and analyses incorporating image properties and behaviour, we found that the pupil singles out illusory faces in a way that differs from previous neural and behavioural measures of these stimuli. We interpret this distinct response as evidence that the pupil is sensitive to the ongoing competition between the face and object interpretations that define face pareidolia.

Our central finding was that pupil responses to illusory faces were neither intermediate between human faces and objects, as might be predicted from spontaneous similarity and face-likeness judgements, nor object-like, as might be predicted from explicit categorisation (Robinson et al., 2025; Wardle et al., 2020). Instead, illusory faces produced pupil dilation while both human faces and non-face objects produced constriction. This non-monotonic pattern is important because it cannot be explained by positioning illusory faces somewhere along a graded face-object continuum: an intermediate response would be consistent with graded face-likeness, whereas an object-like response would be consistent with explicit categorisation and the later neural representation of these stimuli. Rather, the pupil distinguishes illusory faces, the one stimulus category for which perceptual identity is contested. Crucially, this dissociation remained after controlling for luminance and emotional valence, despite luminance being by far the strongest determinant of pupil size in the dataset. Thus, the pupil response cannot be explained simply by differences in these image properties.

Together, these findings suggest that the pupil is sensitive to something not captured by measures of perceptual identity alone. Previous neural and behavioural measures have largely characterised how an illusory face is represented or perceived as being face-like, object-like, or somewhere between the two (Robinson et al., 2025; Wardle et al., 2020). The pupil instead appears to be sensitive to the coexistence of the competing face and object interpretations. What distinguishes illusory faces may not only be where they fall along the face-object continuum, but the fact that their perceptual identity remains contested even after the object interpretation dominates the visual representation. The pupil's non-luminance response is a general arousal index, and arousal could have many causes including perceptual conflict, novelty, attentional capture, effort, and interest among them (Bradley et al., 2008; Mathôt, 2018; Sirois & Brisson, 2014). Given its relatively early onset (~350 ms), the illusory-face dilation most plausibly reflects parasympathetic inhibition via the Edinger-Westphal nucleus rather than slower sympathetic or locus-coeruleus-driven activity (Widmann et al., 2018). Although the current design cannot fully dissociate the cause of this effect, our graded analyses constrain which accounts are most plausible. First, the illusory-face effect did not diminish with repeated exposure, making an explanation based on novelty or surprise unlikely. Second, within the illusory-face set, pupil dilation increased with the probability that an image was categorised as a face, and to a lesser extent with rated face-likeness. Thus, the stronger the competing face interpretation, the greater the pupil response. Importantly, however, illusory faces produced greater dilation than real faces, indicating that the response cannot simply reflect the strength of a face signal or the attentional salience of faces (Conway et al., 2008). Instead, we propose that pupil dilation reflects the extent to which the face interpretation competes with the veridical object interpretation. In other words, the more strongly a face is perceived within an object, the greater the unresolved competition between these two identities. Thus, these findings favour a conflict interpretation over novelty, surprise, or simple salience. This bears directly on the paradox motivating the work. Electrophysiological studies of face pareidolia indicate a rapid shift in the dominant neural representation: the face-like representation dominates early, from roughly 90-130 ms, and is overtaken by an object-like representation by 150-210 ms, after which the object structure persists (Robinson et al., 2025; Wardle et al., 2020). The pupil effect reported here does not begin until roughly 350 ms and peaks after 600 ms. These latencies should not be compared directly, given the typical speed of the pupil and the fact that they were measured in different studies and observers. Nevertheless, the pupil response provides no evidence that illusory faces simply become equivalent to objects once the object-like neural representation becomes dominant. Instead, illusory faces remain strongly differentiated from both unambiguous categories. If the initial face interpretation was simply corrected, and subsequently disregarded, we might expect downstream responses to converge on those elicited by objects. Yet, the pupil shows the opposite pattern, where illusory faces elicit a response that is more distinct from objects than the response elicited by real faces, despite their veridical object identity.

Together these findings point to a division of labour whereby visual representations may settle quickly on appropriate interpretations of a stimulus to guide behaviour, while competing perceptual interpretations continue to be considered and maintained. This fits the multiplexed-representation account proposed for these stimuli, on which the initial face interpretation is not fully overwritten but maintained alongside the object interpretation (Robinson et al., 2025). Maintaining two incompatible interpretations of a single stimulus may carry an ongoing processing cost, and the pupil may provide an index of this competition rather than of either perceptual identity. From this perspective, asking when face pareidolia, as a visual illusion, is "resolved" might be the wrong question. The ambiguity is resolved in the sense that the visual system arrives at the "correct" identity and this solution will dominate perceptual judgements and behavioural decisions. However, these findings indicate that the "incorrect" face interpretation continues to compete for resources and its percept persists. As such, the experience of face pareidolia reveals that the dominant visual representation does not dictate the limits of what we see.
